title: Prove an Opportunity Is Worth Pursuing
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article offers a discipline for deciding whether to chase a big opportunity: identify the one or two critical facts or premises that must be true for the opportunity to actually pay off, then work deliberately to prove or disprove them before committing. It walks through the standard calculus leaders use when sizing up an opportunity — fit, trusted validation, upside versus downside — but argues rarity itself is a trap, since scarcity alone can create fear-of-missing-out pressure to chase something poorly vetted. Using an acquisition example, the piece shows how naming the make-or-break fact (such as hidden liabilities) turns a vague gut call into a testable decision.
points: The core technique is identifying the specific fact or premise that must hold true for an opportunity to be worth pursuing, then actively working to prove or disprove it.
Rarity of an opportunity is named as a trap in itself — scarcity can push leaders toward fear-of-missing-out decisions rather than sound analysis.
A worked acquisition example (hidden debt, liabilities, or litigation) shows how naming the critical fact converts a vague instinct into a testable, falsifiable decision.
The article's closing framing — "real hair on the dog" — warns that opportunities often look more one-sided or asymmetrical than they actually are.
quotes: The decision to pursue a big opportunity can prove to be a game-changer or a time sink of disappointment.
They know that to smartly pursue any opportunity, they must first believe one or more critical facts.
Every opportunity has one or more key facts and premises that are essential for the potential of the opportunity to be realized.
Good leaders identify those facts and premises early and then work hard to prove or disprove them.
Opportunity often comes disguised as one-sided or asymmetrical when, in fact, there is real hair on the dog, as they say.
Decide what premise needs to be determined before taking the leap. You will fall on your face less often as a result.
